data.title: Week 3 Lecture, Part 2: Quantifiers
data.subtitle: Lead-in, Activity 1 and Activity 2 with solutions

narr: Welcome to Week 3 Lecture, Part 2, where we'll explore quantifiers in English. These are words that tell us how much or how many of something there is. Let's start with a lead-in activity to get us thinking.
In the lead-in activity, you'll hear sentences with missing words. Your task is to complete them after listening. Let's look at the sentences you'll be working with.

data.heading: Problem 1 — Lead-in Sentences
data.problem: Complete the sentences with the missing quantifiers:
steps: I used to have ________ of different gadgets, but now I use my phone for almost everything.
I'd like to have a better computer, but I don't have ________ to buy one right now.
I spend ________ time online. I think I need to take a break.
I have a lot of friends on social media, but only ________ of them are close friends.
I never watch TV or films on my phone, because the screen isn't ________.
I like Apple products, but I can't afford them — I think they're ________.
data.result: Answers: (1) a lot (of); (2) enough money; (3) too much; (4) a couple (or a few); (5) big enough; (6) too expensive.

narr: These sentences recycle important quantifier rules from our catalogue: a lot of, enough, too much, and too + adjective.
After listening to the recording, you should have completed the sentences with the correct quantifiers.
Let's move on to Activity 1, where you'll practice choosing between different quantifiers.

data.heading: Problem 2 — Activity 1: Circle the correct option
data.problem: Choose the correct quantifier. Tick if both are possible.
steps: My husband has too much / too many gadgets → too many (countable plural).
I just have to reply to a few / a little emails.
Do you spend much / many time on social media?
My bedroom is a nice size. There's enough room / plenty of room for a desk.
I know very few / very little people who speak two foreign languages.
My brother has downloaded a lot of / lots of apps onto his new phone.

narr: In this activity, pay attention to whether nouns are countable or uncountable, and remember the special rules for questions and negative sentences.

data.heading: Problem 2 — Activity 1: Circle the correct option (cont.)
steps: I have some cash on me, but not a lot / a lot of.
Their new TV is too much big / too big. It hardly fits in the living room.
There aren't any / There are no potatoes. I forgot to buy some.
My niece isn't old enough / enough old to play with a games console.
I don't have a lot of / many close friends.
data.result: Answers: (1) a few; (2) much; (3) both possible; (4) very few; (5) both possible; (6) a lot; (7) too big; (8) both possible; (9) old enough; (10) both possible.

narr: Some items have more than one possible correct answer, which shows how flexible quantifiers can be in different contexts.
Now let's try Activity 2, where you'll identify and correct errors in highlighted phrases.

data.heading: Problem 3 — Activity 2: Identify and correct errors
data.problem: Are the highlighted phrases right (✓) or wrong (X)? Correct the wrong ones.
steps: My nephew got lots of video games for his birthday. ✓
I don't post much photos online. → many photos
'How many presents did you get?' 'A lot of!' → A lot!
I buy fewer e-books than I used to because I prefer physical books. ✓
There isn't no time to walk there. We'll have to get a taxi. → There isn't any time / There's no time
Please turn that music down. It's too much loud! → too loud

narr: Notice how some errors involve double negatives, which are not standard in English.

data.heading: Problem 3 — Activity 2: Identify and correct errors (cont.)
steps: There aren't many good programmes on TV tonight. ✓
My broadband isn't enough fast for me to download films easily. → isn't fast enough
I get too much emails at work. It takes me ages to read them all! → too many emails
A: How much fruit do we have? B: Any. Can you buy some? → None
There are only a little people that I can talk to about my problems. → only a few people
Katarina has plenty of money, so she always has the latest phone. ✓
data.result: These exercises help reinforce important rules like avoiding double negatives and placing quantifiers correctly in sentences.

narr: Others show the importance of placing 'enough' correctly - after adjectives, but before nouns.
Let's now move to Part 3 of our lecture, which focuses on reading about organizing digital lives.

data.title: Week 3 Lecture, Part 3: Reading
data.subtitle: "8 ways to tidy up your digital life"

narr: In Part 3, we'll explore an article about digital organization. Before reading, let's consider some questions about our own digital habits.
The article discusses how to manage our digital lives more effectively, covering topics like email organization, app management, photo storage, and social media connections.

data.heading: Problem 4 — Digital Life Self-Assessment
data.problem: Work with a partner and answer these questions about your digital organization:
steps: Who has a more organized digital life?
Approximately how many emails do you have in your inbox? Do you organize them into folders?
How often do you add new apps on your phone or delete old ones?
How many photos do you have on your phone? Are they organized into albums? How quickly could you find a photo you wanted to show someone?
How many friends do you have on social media? How many of them are real friends? Do you ever unfollow anyone?
data.result: These questions help reflect on personal digital habits before reading the article about organization strategies.

narr: Take a moment to discuss these questions with a partner. Your answers will help you connect personally with the material in the article.
After this self-assessment, you'll be ready to read the article about digital organization and apply its suggestions to your own digital life.
